prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalyzed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling, making the construction of aryl amines a predictable catalytic reaction

statement.case_for: I have moved from halide perovskites (B056) to palladium-catalyzed C-N cross-coupling. The round-1 exchange shows that B065 is the only candidate on which the proponents agree on both topic and allocation: Buchwald and Hartwig developed, in parallel and independently, general ligand-controlled catalytic amination, supported by serious mechanistic work on amine binding and C-N reductive elimination. Three decades of independent use in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and materials synthesis settle maturity and confirmation, and a two-name prize needs no forced omission. The 2010 overlap is real, but C-N reductive elimination from palladium amido complexes is a different mechanistic problem from the C-C couplings that prize recognised, and the citation can say so by naming the formation of C-N bonds and the ligand design behind it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that the 2010 prize for Heck, Negishi and Suzuki already covers the principle, so C-N coupling may be read as an extension rather than a new concept. Kosugi's and Migita's earlier tin-amide work is a genuine precursor, and credit for successive ligand generations is contestable. It is also a synthetic-methodology tool and not a new materials class, which I value, and I give up that argument for B056 for now because it has not found support beyond Linke's ranking and a minority view that the field is early.

responses.point: Johan Aqvist would wait on halide perovskites until stability is clearer, regarding this as timing and not a scientific objection, and says that C-N coupling is a mechanistically novel ligand-controlled method that is distinct from the 2010 prize.
responses.response: I accept the timing point on perovskites: operational stability and lead toxicity are open, and the credit is spread over at least six groups, so any trio is arguable. I also find your mechanistic argument for B065 persuasive. Difficult reductive elimination from palladium amido species, controlled by ligand design, is a distinct problem from the C-C couplings of 2010, and it gives the citation a defensible statement of novelty. That is the main reason I now prefer B065.

responses.point: Peter Somfai argues that C-N coupling is a completely matured, new reaction class with unusually clean two-person attribution, and that perovskites should be held for a later year.
responses.response: I agree with your maturity and attribution argument and I withdraw my round-1 reservation that the allocation is not clean. I did note that Hartwig also appears in your C-H functionalisation trio, but that is an alternative and not part of your preferred configuration, so it does not create a competing duplicate. On the Kosugi and Migita precursor, I would leave them to the citation wording, with 'general' as the operative word, since their tin-amide reaction lacked the generality and catalyst design that Buchwald and Hartwig supplied.

responses.point: Peter Brzezinski prefers targeted protein degradation with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, and says that B065 would be the safer choice if the PROTAC and glue strands cannot be reconciled.
responses.response: I still think the concept of B026 is original and independently confirmed, and I keep it as an alternative. My objection is attribution: the PROTAC strand (Crews, Deshaies, Ciulli) and the cereblon glue strand (Handa, Ito, Gray) are separate achievements, and your own against-case says the trio could look like two discoveries in one citation. You describe B065 as the safer choice in that case, and I think that is where the committee stands. A two-part B026 would need more than three names, which the cap does not allow.

responses.point: Andrei Chabes argues that B065 is the cleanest case on discovery, mechanism and impact, that a two-person prize avoids forced omissions, and that the committee could turn against it on the 2010 overlap.
responses.response: In round 1 I said the citation must explain why this is not an extension of the 2010 award. I think the wording 'general' and 'carbon-nitrogen' does that, and I agree with you that the general ligand-controlled method is distinct enough. I also share your point on omissions: most other candidates would force a cut from five to eight names, and B065 does not.

responses.point: Heiner Linke prefers massively parallel sequencing with Balasubramanian and Klenerman and asks whether it is accepted as chemistry after the 1980 sequencing prize.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked how you weigh the earlier sequencing prizes. Your answer, that the case rests on reversible-terminator chemistry and cluster readout, is clear and the Solexa pair is a clean allocation. But five members, including you, name the chemistry-versus-genomics concern, and I cannot settle it better than you can. I would not move to B037, and I leave it outside my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether a majority will accept that C-N coupling is conceptually distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize, or whether it will read as a refinement
Whether Kosugi or Migita should appear in the citation wording, since the two-name allocation leaves them out

Whether a perovskite prize in a later year would be better placed once stability and toxicity data are clearer, and which three of Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Seok, Gratzel and Kanatzidis would then be named
Whether B026 will be accepted before any PROTAC approval, and how the PROTAC and glue strands would be allocated
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for palladium-catalyzed C-N coupling, halide perovskites or targeted protein degradation. My field of electron crystallography and porous materials is close to candidates that are not on this shortlist, and I am a Stockholm University colleague of Secretary Peter Brzezinski, which is a professional and not a scientific connection. My change of preference away from B056 is not due to any such link, and no recusal is needed.
